graphicEarnsIt.says: Five small dot-grids, each with as many dots as the label under it (31 themes, 22 backgrounds, 31 looks, 26 cuts, 35 stings), strung together with multiplication signs and resolving to 19.2M. The picture shows a combinatorial explosion: five modest, countable sets of choices whose product is an enormous number of possible outputs from one file. The point of drawing it is that the ingredient counts are small enough to take in at a glance, which is what makes the 19.2M land. RIGHT has no graphic at all on this or any beat; its equivalent claim is a line of type, so for RIGHT the honest answer is 'nothing, it is decoration' and there is not even decoration.

A combinatorial explosion made countable. Five small dot matrices stand for five independent choices in the system (31 themes, 22 backgrounds, 31 looks, 26 cuts, 35 stings), each grid holding roughly as many dots as its label, joined by multiplication signs and resolving to 19.2M. The picture shows WHY the number is large: a handful of small menus, multiplied, not one big menu. The dots also do a second job, they make five modest numbers feel small next to the huge one, which is the whole point. RIGHT's frame encodes nothing, it is the same arithmetic written out as a caption.

Combinatorial size, shown by counting rather than asserting. Five blue dot arrays stand for the parts of the system, and each array holds exactly as many dots as its label says: 31 themes (six across, five down, plus one), 22 backgrounds, 31 looks, 26 cuts, 35 stings. Multiplication signs sit between them, so the eye can see five small piles of dots turning into 19.2M at the end of the row. The picture makes the point the words cannot, that the number is not a marketing figure but a product of five small, countable inventories. RIGHT has no graphic at all in any beat: its equivalent claim is a line of type, so for RIGHT the answer is 'nothing, it is decoration' and there is not even decoration.
